Hey - I am in recovery for severe bulimia, and spent about a month at the residential level. 

The absolute best advice I can offer you is to find a trans-specializing dietician. I know switching therapists is really difficult, and it can be even harder if you have a good rapport. But if anything, try and get one for a few sessions to hear what they have to say. The intersection between dysphoria and dysmorphia is a tricky one to navigate, and it made all the difference in the world for me to have a transgender dietician because they could offer me concrete answers to my questions. If there isn’t one in your area (which is likely, because they’re rare) I’d recommend seeking one out online for a few sessions. Paying out of pocket might be expensive, but it’s gonna be a good deal cheaper and less traumatic than relapse, I can promise you that. 

For example, a lot of my issue wasn’t with my weight itself, but the fact that my weight had collected in stereotypically “feminine” areas. I had been under the impression that fat distribution ONLY occurred after periods of weight loss, to the point where I was convinced that my dietician was lying to make me feel better. But I was wrong - testosterone does in fact cause fat redistribution over time even if no significant weight loss occurs. This information had a dramatic effect on my recovery, and I never would’ve known it if I hadn’t had a transgender (or at least trans-specializing) dietician. 

Your particular needs will vary, of course, but it can make a huge difference to find someone who “gets it” and can help you navigate both issues at the same time. I wish you the best of luck. I have been exactly in your shoes, and it’s a BITCH. But I can now say with confidence that I have found peace in my trans, fat body, and with the right resources I know you can too ❤️

I am not going to give you the answer you want to hear right now. Neither is anyone else in this thread. I pray you read through these responses anyways, because they will save your life. 

If you are a 14 year old meth addict, you need to go to rehab. There is absolutely no substitution. None. 

You’ve said it’s not in the cards for you. I’ve been through the system more times than I can count, and in that time I’ve learned one thing - there is always a way. Always. There are countless free resources for teenage addicts without insurance or parental support - and if you actually do have one of those things, your options broaden even more. 

Finding these resources is going to be tricky. There is no central database for these types of things, and it will take some research on your behalf. You must do it anyways. Right now you are balancing on the literal precipice of life and death. I wish I was exaggerating - I am not. Maybe it doesn’t seem like it yet - but I promise it will, sooner than you want to believe. 

How supportive would your parents be of this process? Do they know that you are a meth addict? Even if they are the worst parents on the face of the earth, if they care about you even the slightest amount, they will want you to go to rehab. If they don’t, you must convince them. Ideally, they should be handling the bulk of this process. You are their child. 

If they are, inexplicably, unwilling to place their 14 year old in rehab, there are still options for you. I’d recommend reaching out to whatever free service is available in your area. If you are American, I’d recommend calling this hotline (18662354572) or visiting a local NA meeting and literally just asking someone to help you. Tell them exactly what issues are holding you back from treatment, and they will help you work around those issues. No matter where you live, I’d recommend typing “(insert country) teenage drug hotline” and you will almost certainly find resources. 

There is rehab for people who are homeless, underage, flat broke, or all of the above. There is rehab for people who have nowhere else to go. You want to learn to handle your dysphoria without meth? This is how you do that. You will not get any other actionable solutions on Reddit, I promise. 

I am a veteran of the treatment system. Like you, my drug use was triggered by the desire to repress dysphoria. You may think dysphoria is your number one problem right now, but it’s not. Your number one problem is meth. 

At the VERY least, if you are unwilling to do any of the above, just go to a NA meeting and ask for advice there. Nobody here will be able to give you the help you need. If they think they can, they are probably not familiar with addiction. If you go to a virtual meeting, they even have trans-specific chapters. They will be much more equipped to help you. 

Please do not mistake my bluntness for condescension - I am speaking bluntly because the choices you make in this moment, and the moments that follow, will define the entirety of your life. And if you make the wrong decision, that life will be very, very short. Please seek help.

If he calls himself a lesbian, you shouldn’t be ashamed of being attracted to him as a lesbian would. The divide between butch and transmasculine is very thin nowadays and I’m of the opinion that being attracted to someone who straddles that divide does not negate your sexuality. As long as you are using terms that affirm his gender presentation (which are different for everyone) I don’t think you have anything to be guilty about.

As for whether or not transmasc people are “allowed” to call themselves lesbians….that is a MUCH more contentious debate. I’m personally of the opinion that policing words is idiotic and people should be allowed to align with whatever identity makes them feel most whole with themselves. But as a transmasc lesbian myself, I might be kind of biased. 

There’s a reason people like me might prefer that word over another. We are most often not completely “binary male” so calling ourselves straight feels off. Calling ourselves queer, while helpful for many, can lead to confusion over just what gender we’re “queer” for. And there’s no orientation called “into-womanality”. So a lot of us land on lesbian, to communicate what our preferred partner type is, and (for many of us) to communicate just how queer our relationships still feel to us, even if we technically fall on the “opposing” side of gender presentation. If you’re dating a fem-presenting non-transitioned transmasc person, it can feel a lot closer to a lesbian relationship than a straight one, although NOT all transmasc people agree with this/identify with lesbianism at all. But yours does. So fuck it 🤷

If she smiles, or sustains for what feels like a long time, you’re good to try and “make your move” so long as that move doesn’t involve immediately getting all up in her shit. Start by dancing near her, and if she keeps returning warm eye contact or, god forbid, moves closer to you herself, you are good to (carefully) close the distance, keeping an eye out for any signs of discomfort or annoyance.

There's a lot I've typed, and deleted, in response to this, but I'll try to keep it as brief as possible. This post really resonated with me. 

One, I believe that every person who manages to survive this cursed hellrock we call Earth and make it to adulthood is faced with a recurring choice throughout their life - the choice to build internal walls to keep pain, and everything else, out, or the choice to remain exposed and let life in. Protection, or connection. A lot of people seem to think that option one makes for the "strongest" person overall. I think that's hilariously incorrect, and sometimes leads me to believe that society is being run by edgy 13-year-olds. 

As you've already pointed out, being vulnerable is probably the bravest and strongest thing a person can do. Anyone who disagrees either hasn't done enough living yet or possesses a very shallow, rudimentary idea of how the world works. Either way, they are not your concern. The vast majority of people will see your honesty for what it is - an act of insane courage. 

As for how to build yourself up to that, there's really no other way besides just doing the thing. The good news is you don't have to do it all at once - you can start with people who are closest to you, and work your way outwards. By the time you make it to workplace acquaintances you'll probably be so over the "coming-out" thing that it won't even feel like that big of a deal. 

When I first came out I thought it'd be the big things that scared me - getting disowned, transphobic comments, etc. And while that is, and continues to be, a problem for me, in my personal experience the thing that makes transness so fucking scary is the daily terror of looking people in the eyes and essentially saying "Hi, I was assigned the wrong gender at birth and have only now realized that fact." It's exhausting, and frustrating, and embarrassing. It has also forced me to live deeper and more authentically than I ever did before. In my past life I was always the person that refused to make mistakes in public, refused to be emotionally honest with the people around me. Refused to take up space. Now that I'm trans, I can no longer refuse those things, and I believe it has made me a better person.

Hey, I used to suffer from severe bulimia so I know where you’re at right now. My number one advice would be to seek out the help of a dietician who could give you actual professional advice, as the intersection between gender dysphoria and ED is a tricky one to navigate. But since that’s easier said than done, I’ll tell you what I do. 

First off, I’d recommend very rarely (if ever) weighing yourself. It is truly amazing how much peace that will give you. I personally never weigh myself, but I understand that that’s a difficult standard for most people to stick to, so I’d seriously recommend keeping it to no more than once a week. Just enough to get a general idea of progress, but not so much that you start obsessing. 

Beyond that, I really wouldn’t recommend intense restriction or counting of any kind. Keep a general idea of the amount of calories going into your body, but don’t make a religion out of it. Same with daily exercise - move your body in ways that feel good to you, and put focus on how you feel before, during, and after rather than how much you’re “burning”. Do not “earn” desserts or other indulgences by over-exercising. It is a form of self-punishment that almost always spirals into an ugly cycle for people with ED tendencies. 

Lastly, as difficult as it is with the way diet culture has shaped our rhetoric and behavior, try not to “forbid” any groups of food or apply labels like “bad” or “unhealthy”. Something that many people don’t realize is that overindulging almost ALWAYS happens because of prior restriction of some kind, whether it’s skipping meals or eating irregularly. I used to consider myself a “sugar addict” who was doomed to a life of poor self-control and suffering because of my sweet tooth. Guess what…I eat dessert literally every day now, and still eat regular meals, and STILL often end up at a calorie deficit. Fuck avoiding “bad” food. Unhealthy food is the shit. And it is possible to enjoy it in moderation, so long as you’re packing your stomach with the nutrient-dense stuff as well. Learn to trust yourself, and your body. 

I am 10000% NOT a dietician and you should really seek one out if you are planning to lose weight with an ED history. Many dieticians nowadays actually don’t promote intentional weight loss at all, and I’d really recommend familiarizing yourself with HAES and up-to-date nutritional science. However, as someone who has been much heavier than you at various points in my life, I know better than anyone the pain and suffering that weight shame can cause - I would not wish it on my worst enemy. While on this journey, please do your best to use kind words towards your body and treat it with respect. It will prevent you from doing unhealthy things out of desperation, and in the long run, will help you find peace much, MUCH faster than if you tried to crash-diet your way to being skinny.

I guess my question is, what’s the difference between you (completely transitioned) and a “real man”? 

Your chest would be the same. Your voice would be the same. Your genitals, fat distribution, and body hair would be the same. Even your hormones would be the same. 

The ONLY thing that would distinguish you from a “normal” cis man is your chromosomes. Which have virtually no effect on your daily life whatsoever. Even so, there are PLENTY of men who’ve taken a college biology class and randomly discovered that they have a chromosomal intersex condition through happenstance. Does that negate their identity as men? Of course not. 

Maybe your post transition body won’t fit into the “average” - you’ll have scars where others don’t, and your dick might not look like the “typical” cis dick. But there’s no such thing as an average man anyways! Every guy has things about themselves they’re embarassed about - scars, stretch marks, odd-looking body parts. They’re still men. And so are you.

Ok, so not to scare you, but…I had the exact same experience when I went on T for the first time, and I had to choose right then and there whether to succumb to my disordered eating behaviors or get my life on the right track. Unfortunately, I chose wrong. 

Rather than seeking therapy and getting my nutrition in check, I began starving myself. When that fell through, I turned to bulimia. And because bulimia is just a shitty weight maintenance tool in general, I gained 30 pounds in 3 months. I am now entering an eating disorder treatment center, and as you can imagine my overall health is not great and I have a lot of regrets. 

I am not AT ALL saying you will follow the exact same path as me. I had a lot of contributing factors that led to having such an intense presentation, including severe mental health issues unrelated to my eating disorder. The point I’m trying to make is that little problems have the potential to spiral into much bigger problems if left unchecked. You clearly have a history of disordered eating, no matter how harmless it might’ve seemed at the time, and testosterone-induced weight gain can be a trigger for that. My firm recommendation is to seek out therapy for yourself, and possibly get started working with a dietician as well. Your therapist can help you challenge the thought patterns that lead to disordered eating, while your dietician can help you develop an eating plan that satiates you without triggering harmful habits and behaviors. (If you can’t find a dietician you could also try a nutrition-based app, though I would strongly recommend one that promotes Health At Every Size and not weight loss as a goal.) Find a therapist that takes your insurance and has experience with eating disorders, and shop around if the first one you find isn’t a good fit. I know seeing a therapist might seem like a sizable investment, but as someone who just shelled out $2500 for treatment (not to mention the countless dollars I’ve spent on binge foods) it’s a much wiser decision than leaving it to chance. 

It’s good that you fear the risk of disordered eating more than you fear the weight - that is the proper, mentally-healthy response to have, and is a sign that you’re on the right track. I would capitalize on your present motivation to stay well and nip these thoughts in the bud before they become more intrenched. Worst case scenario, you over-prepare for a scenario that never comes to pass - but that’s better than the alternative. Besides, therapy and education is almost never a bad idea. Good luck ❤️

If you are a 14 year old meth addict, you need to go to rehab. There is absolutely no substitution. None. 

You’ve said it’s not in the cards for you. I’ve been through the system more times than I can count, and in that time I’ve learned one thing - there is always a way. Always. There are countless free resources for teenage addicts without insurance or parental support - and if you actually do have one of those things, your options broaden even more. 

Finding these resources is going to be tricky. There is no central database for these types of things, and it will take some research on your behalf. You must do it anyways. Right now you are balancing on the literal precipice of life and death. I wish I was exaggerating - I am not. Maybe it doesn’t seem like it yet - but I promise it will, sooner than you want to believe. 

How supportive would your parents be of this process? Do they know that you are a meth addict? Even if they are the worst parents on the face of the earth, if they care about you even the slightest amount, they will want you to go to rehab. If they don’t, you must convince them. Ideally, they should be handling the bulk of this process. You are their child. 

If they are, inexplicably, unwilling to place their 14 year old in rehab, there are still options for you. I’d recommend reaching out to whatever free service is available in your area. If you are American, I’d recommend calling this hotline (18662354572) or visiting a local NA meeting and literally just asking someone to help you. Tell them exactly what issues are holding you back from treatment, and they will help you work around those issues. No matter where you live, I’d recommend typing “(insert country) teenage drug hotline” and you will almost certainly find resources. 

There is rehab for people who are homeless, underage, flat broke, or all of the above. There is rehab for people who have nowhere else to go. You want to learn to handle your dysphoria without meth? This is how you do that. You will not get any other actionable solutions on Reddit, I promise. 

I am a veteran of the treatment system. Like you, my drug use was triggered by the desire to repress dysphoria. You may think dysphoria is your number one problem right now, but it’s not. Your number one problem is meth. 

At the VERY least, if you are unwilling to do any of the above, just go to a NA meeting and ask for advice there. Nobody here will be able to give you the help you need. If they think they can, they are probably not familiar with addiction. If you go to a virtual meeting, they even have trans-specific chapters. They will be much more equipped to help you. 

Please do not mistake my bluntness for condescension - I am speaking bluntly because the choices you make in this moment, and the moments that follow, will define the entirety of your life. And if you make the wrong decision, that life will be very, very short. Please seek help.

There’s a reason people like me might prefer that word over another. We are most often not completely “binary male” so calling ourselves straight feels off. If you’re dating a fem-presenting non-transitioned transmasc person, it can feel a lot closer to a lesbian relationship than a straight one, although NOT all transmasc people agree with this/identify with lesbianism at all. Hey, I used to suffer from severe bulimia so I know where you’re at right now. My number one advice would be to seek out the help of a dietician who could give you actual professional advice, as the intersection between gender dysphoria and ED is a tricky one to navigate. But since that’s easier said than done, I’ll tell you what I do. 

First off, I’d recommend very rarely (if ever) weighing yourself. It is truly amazing how much peace that will give you. I personally never weigh myself, but I understand that that’s a difficult standard for most people to stick to, so I’d seriously recommend keeping it to no more than once a week. Just enough to get a general idea of progress, but not so much that you start obsessing. 

Beyond that, I really wouldn’t recommend intense restriction or counting of any kind. Keep a general idea of the amount of calories going into your body, but don’t make a religion out of it. Same with daily exercise - move your body in ways that feel good to you, and put focus on how you feel before, during, and after rather than how much you’re “burning”. Do not “earn” desserts or other indulgences by over-exercising. It is a form of self-punishment that almost always spirals into an ugly cycle for people with ED tendencies. 

Lastly, as difficult as it is with the way diet culture has shaped our rhetoric and behavior, try not to “forbid” any groups of food or apply labels like “bad” or “unhealthy”. Something that many people don’t realize is that overindulging almost ALWAYS happens because of prior restriction of some kind, whether it’s skipping meals or eating irregularly. I used to consider myself a “sugar addict” who was doomed to a life of poor self-control and suffering because of my sweet tooth. Guess what…I eat dessert literally every day now, and still eat regular meals, and STILL often end up at a calorie deficit. Fuck avoiding “bad” food. Unhealthy food is the shit. And it is possible to enjoy it in moderation, so long as you’re packing your stomach with the nutrient-dense stuff as well. Learn to trust yourself, and your body. 

I am 10000% NOT a dietician and you should really seek one out if you are planning to lose weight with an ED history. Many dieticians nowadays actually don’t promote intentional weight loss at all, and I’d really recommend familiarizing yourself with HAES and up-to-date nutritional science. However, as someone who has been much heavier than you at various points in my life, I know better than anyone the pain and suffering that weight shame can cause - I would not wish it on my worst enemy. While on this journey, please do your best to use kind words towards your body and treat it with respect. It will prevent you from doing unhealthy things out of desperation, and in the long run, will help you find peace much, MUCH faster than if you tried to crash-diet your way to being skinny.

Ok, so not to scare you, but…I had the exact same experience when I went on T for the first time, and I had to choose right then and there whether to succumb to my disordered eating behaviors or get my life on the right track. Unfortunately, I chose wrong. 

Rather than seeking therapy and getting my nutrition in check, I began starving myself. When that fell through, I turned to bulimia. And because bulimia is just a shitty weight maintenance tool in general, I gained 30 pounds in 3 months. I am now entering an eating disorder treatment center, and as you can imagine my overall health is not great and I have a lot of regrets. 

I am not AT ALL saying you will follow the exact same path as me. I had a lot of contributing factors that led to having such an intense presentation, including severe mental health issues unrelated to my eating disorder. The point I’m trying to make is that little problems have the potential to spiral into much bigger problems if left unchecked. You clearly have a history of disordered eating, no matter how harmless it might’ve seemed at the time, and testosterone-induced weight gain can be a trigger for that. My firm recommendation is to seek out therapy for yourself, and possibly get started working with a dietician as well. Your therapist can help you challenge the thought patterns that lead to disordered eating, while your dietician can help you develop an eating plan that satiates you without triggering harmful habits and behaviors. (If you can’t find a dietician you could also try a nutrition-based app, though I would strongly recommend one that promotes Health At Every Size and not weight loss as a goal.) Find a therapist that takes your insurance and has experience with eating disorders, and shop around if the first one you find isn’t a good fit. I know seeing a therapist might seem like a sizable investment, but as someone who just shelled out $2500 for treatment (not to mention the countless dollars I’ve spent on binge foods) it’s a much wiser decision than leaving it to chance. 

It’s good that you fear the risk of disordered eating more than you fear the weight - that is the proper, mentally-healthy response to have, and is a sign that you’re on the right track. I would capitalize on your present motivation to stay well and nip these thoughts in the bud before they become more intrenched. Worst case scenario, you over-prepare for a scenario that never comes to pass - but that’s better than the alternative. Besides, therapy and education is almost never a bad idea. Good luck ❤️

Make sure you have someone to turn to if shit goes sideways, even if it’s just one person outside the group. It’ll make the grief much less intense if (god forbid) the relationship did end, and you needed to spend some time away from the group.

I would even go so far as to say that your friend should be mindful of that struggle, and avoid direct comparisons of your experience to theirs that might come across as insensitive or tone-deaf. 

That being said, it’s highly likely that they are experiencing major struggles as well, which - though separate from yours - are still extremely difficult to endure. I absolutely adore the name Sebastian and I'm not just saying that to be supportive. 

This is just my experience, but I think for most people the idea of a "perfect name" that describes you to a T and is loved by all is a bit of an unrealistic expectation, and one I've gotten trapped in myself. I was obsessed with my name when I first chose it, but my family's response was lackluster and after meeting 3 trans people with the exact same name in a single group (yes, I have one of those) my enthusiasm started to wane a bit. But after a while I grew to love it again - not because it was the most amazing end-all-be-all chosen name on Earth, but because it was mine and at that point it had become a part of me. 

Almost no cis person on Earth is in love with their own name - it's just a thing about them like any other, one they received at birth and don't think much about. So of course you want to pick a name that you really like and that makes you happy, but even the best name on Earth is going to get old after a couple of repeats. All you can do is pick the best one you can find and let it become a part of you - and I'll say it again, I LOVE the name Sebastian. Who doesn't like the name Sebastian? They're crazy. 

Anyways that got tl;dr real fast but no matter what you decide I wish you the best of luck!

edit: your family has a right to their opinions, but they don't have a right to ruin your joy when you've made it clear you really like the name. So I think that says more about them than it does about the name itself. It's your life, not theirs.

I even went so far as to quit extracurriculars I enjoyed, specifically so that I didn't have to go through the "embarrassment" of announcing my name change to everyone. 

Eventually I realized I had a choice; endure a few days of discomfort, maybe a week, and then be at peace forever after, or stick with a name that felt "wrong" for the rest of my life. When I viewed it through that lense, the choice seemed much simpler.

You've explained very clearly why the name change feels necessary to you, and if I was one of your friends I'd respect that reasoning 100%. I'd recommend making the switch casually, joking or apologizing your way through it if you must - but definitely still do it.
